directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can run locally (or copy into your CI pipeline) to finish the tasks you described.  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the remote repo from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create/update files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
We’ll create a minimal Dockerfile that:

| Step | Command |
|------|---------|
| Base image | `python:3.10-slim` (but we’ll keep Node, so use `node:18-alpine`) |
| Install dependencies | `npm ci` |
| Expose port | `3000` |
| Entrypoint | `node app.js` |

**Dockerfile**

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

We’ll create a single `k8s.yaml` that contains both a Deployment and a Service.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip:** If you want the service to be reachable from outside the cluster, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port` accordingly.

Save this as `k8s.yaml` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow that builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub (or any registry), and optionally deploys to a Kubernetes cluster.

```yaml
name: Build & Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'latest'

      - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
        env:
          KUBE_CONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64 encoded kubeconfig
        run: |
          echo "$KUBE_CONFIG_DATA" | base64 -d > kubeconfig
          export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/kubeconfig
          kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

> **Secrets required:**
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (or any other registry credentials)
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – Base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want to deploy automatically.

Save this as `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/deploy.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see the new workflow run in the **Actions** tab of your GitHub repo.  
The Docker image will be built and pushed to Docker Hub (or your chosen registry).  
If you have a Kubernetes cluster configured in the workflow, the deployment will be applied automatically.

That’s it! 🎉
